newsitem.title: USA: Storms boost U.S. Northwest hydropower output.
newsitem.headline: Storms boost U.S. Northwest hydropower output.

text.p: Hydroelectric power turbines in the U.S. Northwest are expected to run at higher rates in coming weeks as water from recent heavy rainstorms is released from reservoirs, industry sources said Friday.

"We expect some recession. Within the next week we hope to get back to long-range targets," said Cindy Henriksen, director of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers reservoir control center in Portland, Ore.
This week reservoirs which were allowed to fill during the recent storms will be drawn down, she added.

The emphasis at dam operations has been on flood control since just after Christmas, when the first of a series of storms hit the region, prompting operators to hold back water at upstream dams along most major Northwest rivers to limit flooding farther downstream.
But forecasts now call for cooler, drier air to continue moving down from Canada, replacing the moist winter storms.
Some concerns have been raised about heavier-than-normal snow melt in the wake of the storms, but Henriksen said runoff volume does not appear to be a problem.
"Some of the snowpack in Idaho is still 200 percent of normal," she said.
Dams in northern and central California are also expected to gear up power generation once flood control needs abate over the next several days.
Output has been curtailed due to heavy spilling and damage to some California dams caused during recent heavy floods.
"They will need to make space for more rain or snow," said one California utility source.
He noted that a lot of water was lost to spilling during the floods. "(But) a lot ran into the reservoirs - they filled them early."
